content: Group 12 elements in the periodic table, as defined by IUPAC, include the transition metals zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), mercury (Hg), and ununbium (Uub). These elements are characterized by relatively low melting and boiling points compared to other groups of transition metals. Notably, these properties decrease as one moves down the group. Mercury, for instance, is liquid at standard room temperature, which is a unique property among metals. The liquid state of mercury and the low melting points of other Group 12 elements can be attributed to the electron configuration of mercury and relativistic effects. Mercury’s electron configuration is 4d10 4f14 5s2 5p6 5d10 6s2. The outermost shell, labeled 6s, is completely filled and is located closer to the nucleus than expected due to relativistic effects. The high positive charge of the nucleus causes some electrons to move at velocities significant enough that special relativity must be considered. This results in an increase in the mass of these electrons and a contraction of the size and energy of the s-orbital. These relativistic effects lead to a tightly bound outer shell of electrons in mercury, which prevents the formation of strong metal-metal bonds. Consequently, mercury exists as a liquid at room temperature. Furthermore, due to its inert outer electrons, mercury vapor behaves similarly to a noble gas and has been referred to as pseudohelium. This behavior contrasts with neighboring elements like gold and thallium, which are solids under similar conditions. Group 12 elements are also relatively resistant to corrosion. This property makes them useful for protective applications, such as galvanizing iron with zinc or electroplating with cadmium, to shield base metals from degradation.
